utterances.text: And my last question about this topic is this: It says here that combatants on the front line belonging to this battalion are protesting about the departure of special groups and units from Mostar and the movement, the large-scale movement of civilians and soldiers towards the north. My question to you is this, whether you knew about the movement towards the north?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had intelligence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know that this was a large-scale movement of people?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And finally, just one more time, Mr. Maric, according to your most sincere opinion, we need to know your opinion in these proceedings. When you organised the army and when you established the HVO, what did you think? What state were you defending by doing that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and all those with whom I co-operated, we all defended the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what do you think, Mr. Maric, about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, my fellow Judges are telling me that you have gone well beyond your time and you must stop now. Is this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my last question, indeed. I believe that the question is important and that's why I'll ask your permission to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, what do you think about the multi-ethnicity of Mostar? Do you think that Mostar should have become an exclusively Croatian city?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, Mostar is only possible as a multi-ethnic city in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is the only way it should exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this brings my examination-in-chief to an end, and I would like to thank you for the additional minutes accorded to me. Mr. Maric, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, before I give the floor to the other Defence teams, who have an hour and a half to put questions to you, we, the Judges are faced with the following problem, which is not a fundamental issue but something which is contained in the indictment and the pre-trial brief. The Prosecution claims that the civilians in East Mostar could not leave the town either by the north or by the south. That is the case put forward by Ms. West when she cross-examined a number of witnesses with maps in support of her case. A while ago we saw a document which stemmed from the ABiH, therefore from the other side, in which General Pasalic clearly was asking the civilian authorities to handle the transport of civilians in the direction of the north and in the direction of the south. It's written down. If General Pasalic wrote this, unless at the time he was totally incompetent, this means that, as far as he was concerned, the civilians could move around. And when you answered Mrs. Alaburic's question, you said that they could move around. What I would like to know is this: A while ago we saw another document in which the 1st Corps in Sarajevo was asked to send over some units. When the ABiH was replenished in unit terms, the ABiH soldiers who arrived in Mostar, how did they manage to reach Mostar? Were they sent there with a parachute or did they use the roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the replenishment of units around Mostar from the direction of north was possible throughout the entire time using the Glogosnica-Glogova access, Bijela, Ravni and Bijelo Polje valley access. With short interruptions that could also be done by the Konjic-Jablanica-Bijela road, and also for a short time it was possible via the hill if you walked for about an hour to the village of Ravno and then took some sort of transportation towards the Bijelo Polje valley. If you regulated the flow of water at the Salakovac hydro-electrical power plant, the BiH forces were given a bypass under the Old Bridge, under the new bridge over Bijela, which was the former road leading from Jablanica and Mostar. So what I'm saying is that if they lowered the level of the water, you could reach the old road which, subject to minor repairs, could be made possible for the passage of special vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your leave, Your Honours, I would like to correct something in the transcript. On page 48, line 18, it says Konjic road; whereas the witness said the highway leading from Konjic via Jablanica to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you were talking about the possibility to -- correction, correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought you were just correcting the transcript and not asking more questions as your time is up. But, Witness, you have said that for a short time, and that is page 48, line 19, for a short time it was possible by the hill if you walked for about an hour. Why do you say for a short time? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about a period after the initial conflicts and the withdrawal of some of the units of the HVO into the area of Bijelo Polje or, rather, the villages above Bijelo Polje. After the 30th of June, for a short period of time after that, the BiH Army could regulate the level of Salakovac lake and thus it could use the road to the Bijela Bridge, took a car to Bijela, and then to -- onwards to the village of Ravno. That's the period that I had in mind, between the 30th of June until sometime around the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more correction that should be made, because it is related to Judge Trechsel's question. The way it's recorded in the transcript, I'm not clear on what the witness said. The witness didn't say "for a short time" but "after a short time." After a short time the second means of communication was opened to the BH Army, and this is what the witness meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now question the Defence teams. I would like to know who's starting. 1D? Any questions from 1D?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Prlic's Defence does not have any questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Stojic's Defence also does not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. General Praljak's Defence or, rather, General Praljak himself, with your leave, does have some questions for this witness. General Praljak has been mentioned in examination-in-chief. In addition to that, he participated in the events himself and he has some specialist knowledge regarding the topic that will be the topic of cross-examination by General Praljak. It is my duty to inform you about the parts of the examination-in-chief that will be tackled by the cross-examination and point to the relevant -- relevancy of such examination. The documents are 3D00455, which refers to paragraph 112 of the indictment, 17.3(i) and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when mentioning the numbers of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is recorded on page 64 of yesterday's transcript. The paragraph in the indictment is 117. That's the one that I mentioned last. And the following document that we will be using is already Exhibit P6365, which refers directly to paragraph 114 of the indictment. This was mentioned yesterday to Judge Antonetti's question when the witness was talking about a document issued by Arif Pasalic, 4D00488, which contains references to the topic of sniping. And furthermore, questions will refer to paragraphs 27, 26, and paragraphs relative to Mostar from 88 to 117. All those topics were contained by the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well then. We will briefly about through some matters in very simple terms in order to simplify the procedure. To start with, let's look at the artillery and the problem of the consumption of artillery ammunition with regard to the target. Could you please look at 3D00455. The document is already an exhibit, as we all know. There are two tables in the document. If you want to destroy 25 per cent of various enemy targets or neutralise them -- or neutralise 80 per cent of the enemy targets -- or, rather, for a target to be destroyed to the extent of 80 per cent. My question is this: After the conflict, after the 30th of June, 1993, what was the main thoroughfare in the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main street in the eastern part of Mostar, in the city, is Tito's street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Marsal Tito Street?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have in that street military installations, command bases or something? What targets did they place in the main street in the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware that there were several military installations in that street used by the BH Army forces, beginning with the SDK building where the command of the 4th Corps was based, then the national theatre, the buildings of the Razvitak company with very large basements, the building of the former JNA's military district near the railway station, and they had a military prison in the 4th primary school. Since that street, Marsal Tito Street, goes on to the south in a parallel line, there is a former camp of the JNA leaning onto it, and it was used during the war by the BH Army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Brigadier, in war, is a military installation a military target?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war, a military installation is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All these buildings that you mentioned and some that you didn't mention, were they located in a densely populated part of town, among civilians?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of these facilities are located in the populated part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now, Brigadier, on the other side at that time I was the commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And Mr. Mico Lasic was the commander of the operation zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993, in the area of Mostar in that operation zone, who was attacking whom and how? Low-level attack, medium attack, intensive attack?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993, HVO units were being attacked by BH Army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll just mention 4D00793, dated 20th September 1993. That's a document where General Pasalic says that the HVO was targeted by his front line artillery. Can you remember that major intensive attack on Hum hill by the BH Army and sweeping towards the Liska Street at the foot of the Hum hill?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was the 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's correct. Now tell me, do you remember whose artillery support did the BH Army have on that day in that attack?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. They had artillery support at least from three sources. They had the support of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Maric, look at these tables here. If I were doing my duty, and Mico Lasic, too, if we gave orders to the artillery to destroy the installations of the BH Army which was attacking us, as you said, their military installations in the town of Mostar, wouldn't we have had to expend thousands and thousands and thousands of shells to achieve an 80-per-cent destruction of these installations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If, from whatever neutral international source that was counting the shells falling on the other side, you were to find out that during five and a half months in the second half of 1993 the eastern side of Mostar was hit by 850 shells, would you consider that random, excessive shelling, or would you say as an artillery shelling that it was the absolute minimum under the circumstances of the BH Army attack?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- yes. I can't say less than minimum, but it is the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct the record. I'd like the interpreters to say exactly the way he says it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying I don't have another word to replace your term, "the minimum of the minimum," to make it even more picturesque. But we didn't even have the minimum of the minimum to approach any standards to destroy the military targets on the BH Army side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did observers of the artillery report that the BH Army, firing from mortars, multiple rocket launchers, et cetera, was active from the very centre of the town, near the hospital, near other civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All observers and all monitoring services reported precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, it's year 1992. To which nation do you belong?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge and under the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were Croats a constituent nation, constituent people?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are not artillery questions. I object to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were a link to the issue of who had the right to Bosnia and Herzegovina, an issue raised by Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I want to ask this: Did we Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina by responding to the referendum make it possible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. Regardless of whether this issue was covered during the direct, it doesn't allow Mr. Praljak to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that you are extremely competent also in constitutional and political matters. We didn't know that to start with but we do know that now. The witness is here to speak about artillery. It would be much more important for him to say -- ask a question about the Old Bridge. If you don't put the question, I will. How is it that the Old Bridge collapsed? Following tank fire, as it were, or from another source? That is far more interested -- interesting than constitutional matters everybody is aware of, including the witness, hence Ms. West's objection. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you were the one who asked the witness whom he was defending and I want to clarify that. Who were we defending? I want to see if Mr. Maric came to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia, from Neverland or some other exotic country, or in 1992 he was defending himself from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who was attacking you, Mr. Maric, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the enemy for the Croatian and Bosniak peoples in the area of Mostar were the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti asked you if Mr. Izetbegovic had an army to send help and defend his side in Mostar, or he considered the Yugoslav People's Army, all the way up to the attack in Sarajevo, an army that would save their people?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, it's the same issue. Just because this was talked about during direct does not allow Mr. Praljak to ask these questions. Move to strike them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking permission to respond. I mean, this is the military issue, the issue of whether there was the army to fight with or there was no army. And Mr. Praljak, as you well all -- as you are all very aware, was involved in that from the very beginning, and this is obviously a relevant point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the witness is allowed to answer, but as to the usefulness of the testimony of this witness, it is something else altogether. I asked the question. You want to revisit the subject. Well, I didn't insist. You can ask your question, but you better move on to something else afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will come to that issue, Your Honour, because I have time for that and very soon. I would just like the witness to answer whether there was any army apart from the HVO at the time that was able to save the people, that is, prevent the penetration of the Yugoslav People's Army westward via Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for a fact there was no other army apart from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who bombed nose in 1992, beginning with April?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How much of Mostar was destroyed in that bombing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the percentage, but an overwhelming majority of buildings were destroyed at that time by the Yugoslav People's Army, including all the bridges in this town on the Neretva River, bridges used by vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On what date did the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, the JNA, expel all the people from the left bank to the right bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When approximately was the operation of the liberation of the right bank of the Neretva, that is, the right start of the Mostar, carried out, because the Serbs had positions on the hills around?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who commanded that operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very shortly afterwards, the Neretva was crossed in the section from the Una River to the north, and before that, from Capljina towards Stolac. In Mostar, who gave the command for the crossing, and who commanded part of that operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many losses did we have? How many dead, how many wounded in that operation? If you don't have exact data, never mind.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have exact figures, but in operations against Serbs we had dozens of losses in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier Maric, how many artillery shells did we have at our disposal at the time the decision was made to cross the Neretva River and liberate the eastern side?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, considering that in documents that it is expressed in combat sets, we had on average one combat set per weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If there had been an agreement with the Serbs, was it an easy military operation, and why did we cross the Neretva if the majority of the population there were Muslims? Why would we have done that if there had been an agreement with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware then, and I'm not aware today that there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: As soon as we liberated the right bank of the Neretva, what happened with approximately 115 Croats and Muslims in Uborak and Sutina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed in what could be qualified as a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: By whom against whom?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs killed Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Old Bridge remained the only one, you say. In the fighting, in the crossing on the eastern side, was the Old Bridge protected with pipes and planks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was that done while there was still fighting going on for the bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who defended the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineering units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who issued the order, while the fighting was still going on, to protect the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. You did, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From that time, from the beginning until the end, did the Serb artillery firing at the west of Mostar and the east of Mostar try to spark a conflict between the HVO and the BH Army all the time up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. The Serb side constantly tried to provoke a conflict between these two armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's clarify. The year 1993, from the moment Mostar was liberated, do you know that the HVO at any level ever planned or indeed attacked or in any way hindered the establishment of the BiH Army in that area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did the BiH Army de facto in the area obtain all the weapons they had from the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, yes, and I can especially confirm that they had received a lot after the operations involving Serbs that I personally distributed in the area from Sarajevo to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go back to the second half of 1993. You yourself told us Vrdi, Jug, Blagaj, Buna, Hum. The attacks by the BiH Army, can they be called skirmishes, as His Honour Judge Antonetti put it, or was it really that large-scale and intensive wartime operations were being conducted for months in that area, and in those operations we defended ourselves and we were being attacked by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Large-scale, intense and fierce attack operations were being conducted by the BiH Army against the positions of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In artillery terms, let's say you have a position on Mount Hum. Could you place a 130-millimetre cannon up there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir, not on Hum. A 130-millimetre cannon cannot exist on Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Which one could you place there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A smaller calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From that position -- I apologise. I apologise. From that position could you see the Old Bridge down the barrel, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From certain positions, yes, you could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If I or anybody else had wanted to do so, would it have been possible for anybody to launch one or two or three shells and destroy the Old Bridge any morning during our conflict with the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it would be possible with three shells, but it would have been possible with ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You -- I would have had to target the middle.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't have that experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was my duty to put the question. Maybe General Petkovic will better suited to ask you that. I beg your pardon? Okay. Okay. Judge Antonetti will ask you the rest. I don't have anything to ask you about the Old Bridge. Whatever I had to say about the Old Bridge I already said it, as we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, a question, a follow-up question on the Old Bridge. You know how important this Old Bridge was, symbolically speaking, and you know that it was destroyed. You know that tank crews were prosecuted, and you also know that the accused in this courtroom are also charged with destroying the Old Bridge. I'm speaking purely in military terms. What happens? How does it happen if the artillery is requested to destroy a bridge? Is that done by way of an order? Are there preparations made for the purpose? Technically speaking, how can that be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the destruction of such a building requires long preparation, starting with observation, selection, the selection of a firing position, the selection of equipment and tools, the selection of adequate ammunition, engineering works, and a lot more other preconditions and especially a very sophisticated set of instruments that would be able to give you the exact distance to such a small facility, and all the other elements that are necessary. In other words, such an exercise would require a lot of actions if one wanted to destroy a building such as a small bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still in military terms, it is -- is it conceivable that a tank could decide to position itself without any orders to do so and starts firing on the Old Bridge? Is this possible in military terms or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it would be possible in military terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the event that it happened the way I've just described, that a tank fired on the Old Bridge without having received any prior order or with an order, but if there is an order I have to see it. So far I have seen no such offered to the effect. But if a tank were to fire without any prior order, what is the command authority supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Urgently, by the fastest possible means of communication, such weaponry should be excluded from use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the day when the bridge collapsed - that was in November 1993 - where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That happened two days or a few days before I was wounded. I was at the command observation duty, the southern part of the front line, some 10 kilometres south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were some 10 kilometres away from Mostar. But let us suppose that General Praljak would have decided to destroy the Old Bridge. I suppose that there would have been written orders. I also suppose that you, possibly, because you were the chief of artillery, you would have been on notice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that the -- that that would have been the case. However, I didn't have any knowledge about anybody on the part of the HVO would have planned or carried out an operation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I assume, and all these are mere hypotheses, if General Praljak had decided for some reason to destroy the Old Bridge, would he then have called the chief of artillery to see with him how best to go about it, to destroy the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that had been the plan, I'm sure that he would have called me, either me or anybody else in that position. If it had been me, I would not have taken upon myself such a duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you hear that the Old Bridge had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On return we came across a lower-ranking officer of the HVO who told us that the Old Bridge had been destroyed, had crumbled, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you react? Did you seek to find out who was responsible for it, how it could have been done without you knowing about it, because if it had had to be destroyed, you should have been resorted to and you would have turned it down, you said. Did you ask your superior command to investigate into the matter? What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the HVO artillery was not tied expressly to the destruction of the Old Bridge, I personally didn't ask for any investigation. However, the bodies in the military district probably had information that the bridge had been destroyed. I don't remember that any investigation took place at the military district level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: The tank fired on the Old Bridge. I'm not saying that it was a tank that destroyed the Old Bridge. We don't know anything about it. We will discuss the matter in due time. But this tank that allegedly fired on and destroyed the Old Bridge, under what command authority would it be, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the -- in Mostar military area there was a tank battalion which had a couple of obsolete tanks which mostly acted towards the prevention of onslaught of the enemy through the areas passable to a tank. Those tanks had very limited mobility. And that tank battalion was subordinated to the commander of the Mostar military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mostar operation zone. Very well. Please continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tanks had nothing whatsoever to do with artillery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Second of all, tanks were primarily subordinated to the commander of the tank battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And he in turn was subordinated to the commander of the military district?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that after the destruction of the Old Bridge there was indeed an investigation which was never completed, and the goal of the investigation was to find out how and what unit shot at the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever read the results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a reference to a couple of names, or maybe three names, of the people who possibly participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at another document, P -- it's a film, and it's an exhibit. P6365. P6365. In that video-clip you will see that the author claims that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rewind. Let's see that woman please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please rewind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Not long afterwards, another emergency. A woman was lying on the riverbank."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. The author of this video-clip claims that that unfortunate woman had been hit by sniping fire on the left bank of the Neretva River and that that sniping fire was opened from the position of the HVO. My question to you, Brigadier, since you are a citizen of Mostar, resident of Mostar, and as an artillery man you had a good overview of the directions from which it could be fired from, the Carina bridge, the customs bridge where that part of the town starts from, the customs bridge there, is -- is there a single place in the western part of the city from which one could observe and see the bank on the left bank of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. I waited for the end of that question to see if it was somehow related to the artillery testimony that this witness gave, but it appears not to be, so I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to respond to this objection. The indictment in paragraph 7 and 8 as well as in 15 and 17 claims and alleges that, amongst others, General Praljak is responsible for everything that happened in Mostar as well as the incidents involving sniping fire. That's number one. Number two, the terrain in Mostar is something that General Praljak is very familiar with because he resided there. He was educated there, and the banks of the River Neretva are very well known to him. And this refers to the part where General Praljak has a personal and specialised knowledge because he personally resided in the area. At the objection put forth by my learned friend Ms. West is not based -- is not founded. Also the witness has very concrete knowledge because he hails from the area of Mostar and he's very familiar with the Neretva River, with the banks of the Neretva River and the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, I will join my learned friend Mrs. Pinter in her response. In keeping with Rule 90(H)(i), a cross-examination can tackle the credibility of the witness, the topics raised by the examination-in-chief as well as the all the other important topics "[In English] ... to the case for the cross-examining party, to the subject matter of that case." [Interpretation] For such a cross-examination, the parties do not have to seek permission from the Trial Chamber. I would like to remind you that based on this role the Trial Chamber has already decided on a submission by General Petkovic's Defence and allow the Prosecution to carry out cross-examination irrespective of the topics that were raised during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, my question is for Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Praljak knows that area and the video, well, that is fine, but we want to know whether the witness does know the area and whether he can add anything, and if it's only to confirm what General Praljak knows already, well, that's something we know about. The question is: What can the witness contribute as regards this video? Colonel, you've heard the question. You have seen a video very briefly. You know those parts. Can you contribute anything or can't you say anything whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not easy for me to watch this video-clip, but I will kindly ask you to rewind and let it run from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Afterwards another emergency. A woman was lying on the riverbank. She'd been doing her family's washing. She was already dead, shot by a Croat sniper."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From the top, please. See the people running. Ten metres away from the edge of the riverbank and -- do you see the right bank of the river Neretva? Do you see the right-hand side of the Neretva riverbank from this place?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It seems that the river is deep --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: "A woman was lying on the riverbank. She'd been doing her family's washing."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Once again you saw the people running. You're familiar with the Neretva River. If you are 10 metres away from the edge of the riverbank you can't see anything. Either this riverbank or the other. This is way I saw things. Maybe you can tell us differently.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, this victim is on the right bank, not on the left bank. Judging by the flow of the river you can see that the water's flowing in the right direction which means that the victim is on the right bank. And during the summer, the Neretva is about 27 metres deep if you're measuring from the Old Bridge, about 23 metres from Tito's bridge, and 22 metres from the Carina bridge. This is a canyon, therefore, and as I am looking back at the positions where the HVO positions were, I cannot allow for the possibility for anybody to be able to see the right bank of the river Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you say that the Neretva is deep, do you mean that this is from the Old Bridge to the level -- to the top level of the water? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. So if the victim is level with the top level of the water, you could not observe that, and you certainly could not open fire from the positions of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does this concern what I asked you? If you're looking from the Carina bridge, could you observe that all the way down to --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way down to the ultimate positions of the HVO in the city of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the Trial Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- switch off the image on the screen. Just one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Excuse me. You are both going much too fast and overlapping and we cannot follow. So could you kindly slow down. sorry for being loud, but I thought it was the only possibility to pull the brake, and you don't have to repeat as much as you would have other wise. Please go ahead. Or resume, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I like passions, I hope to inspire even more, especially with an image like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: One more question. If a sniper killed that woman, why isn't he shooting at the soldier you see here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no [Realtime transcript read in error "to"] clever answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this video is a video we've seen already on several occasions. This is a video which, of course, does give rise to an emotional shock when you see this woman washing her family washing and being shot at. We don't know who did this but the commentator says that it is the HVO. I didn't quite understand Mr. Praljak's questions in the beginning, but your answers seem to indicate that, as far as you were concerned, it was impossible for this woman to be shot by an HVO sniper because from the positions of the HVO, it was not possible to hit anyone from there, that particular location. Is that exactly what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You couldn't hit anyone on the right bank, not even the left bank, but especially not the right bank, because it's evident from this image that the victim is on the right bank of the Neretva River. The Neretva flows from the north to the south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're positive about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: There is obvious mistake in transcript and I think this is the reason for your question, Judge Antonetti. In line 8, witness answered, "I don't have clever answer to this question." And it was put in transcript, "I have to clever answer to that question."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. Witness, maybe Ms. Alaburic will help us because I see there is map somewhere in this file of Mostar, and if we -- if you look at it, I would be interested to know whether you can say where this woman has been lying. Can you tell us the number of the document which is the city map of Mostar? I have seen it, but I've not remembered where.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the maps of Mostar we had prepared for you are not very good for this purpose. We have a so-called tourist map of Mostar indicating targets that we prepare for the examination around the 9th of May. It's in your binder. This is the map which is easy for everyone. I can give this map to the witness and he can mark it on the ELMO, but I think it's better to ask him first whether he's able to locate at all the place where the woman is lying, or he can just say on which bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you've heard what Mrs. Alaburic has said. The problem we face is this: On the basis of what you saw and on the basis of the tourist map, would you be able to shed some light on this issue for my fellow Judge? Would you be able to tell us, according to you, where this woman was lying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a technical point for -- for everyone else, the document is 4D00918, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I go get my bag to bring photographs of Mostar so the man can tell us whether this place can be seen from any building in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think even these photographs are necessary for me to answer this question. Ninety-five per cent and perhaps even 100 per cent of the Neretva riverbank on both the right-hand side and the left-hand side are not developed. It's mostly rocks, caves, grottos that look alike at whichever section you look. There are dozens of similar places along the bank and hardly anyone in Mostar, apart from someone born precisely in that spot, could locate exactly one it is, not on the basis of one or two rocks. We need a broader picture to locate this. Ninety-five per cent of the banks are undeveloped, and you can bathe in the Neretva in only two or three places. At least it's allowed in only two or three places. Otherwise, it's too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be unable to locate this spot. Fine. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I only wanted to show the photograph not to locate this place precisely - I know it can't be done - but to show that what you said is correct; namely, that it's impossible to see that river from the buildings. No sniper sitting on top of a building can see the river.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General, I gave an oath to say what I know, and I confirm that it is true. It was impossible from HVO positions, even in peacetime when you could choose your position, it's impossible to see the right bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Last question and last topic. This road from Mostar towards Jablanica and Bijelo Polje is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General Praljak. We shall have a break now because it is 20 minutes to 1.00. Is this your last question, General Praljak? If that is the case, we shall have a break after -- after that, or do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the attack by the BH Army on the 30th of June, was that road passable, continuously passable towards the north, except for one small section, considering that the BH Army controlled it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So the mountain tracks were the only way if anybody wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have shall have a 20-minute break and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak was finished. 5D? Does Mr. Coric's Defence have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we start, just a small correction to the transcript. Page 73, line 16. The question of General Praljak records: "[In English] So the mountain tracks were the only way if anybody wanted to go." Actually, the question was -- of Mr. Praljak the question was: "So the mountain tracks were the parallel or alternative way if anybody wanted to go," and that is what witness then confirmed yes, and that was what was said on Croatian in original and that's how the witness understood the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It has now been recorded as such. 5D, do you have any questions? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6D?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, so you have your three hours. You can begin. We all have received the folders.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber your exact address in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, my address was Mostar, Blajburskih Zrtava 92, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what neighbourhood was that in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the western part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is there a specific name to the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bihovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did the name of that street ever change or is it still known as that today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1992, it was called Prekomorskih Brigada, Overseas Brigade Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you live in a single-family home or in an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a single-family home. In a house.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were any of your neighbours Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Muslim neighbour was about 120 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you give us their name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were more than one. Kajan is one name.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you give us another name, please?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but it will come back to me in a while if you will come back to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in May of 1993, can you tell us where your office was located?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1993, my office was in the command of the military district of Mostar. The building was called Lesnina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was the address of the building?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't answer that question precisely. We'll come across that street in documents perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. Did the location of your office change for the rest of 1993 or did it remain in the same building?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very end of 1993 my office moved to Rudnik, a settlement called Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during the period of 1993, during most days did you work out of your office?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job description required me to spend most of my time at the office, but sometimes on commander's orders I could go on field missions as commander in reconnaissance, mainly in co-operation with the commander of the command concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to go back - we're about to lose it on the transcript - when you gave us your address. It doesn't appear that the street name was spelled out. Can you spell out your street name, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: P-l-a-j-p-u-r-c -- sorry, s --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness just say the name again without -- we don't know where one word begins and the other ends.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, maybe say it one more time and they can try saying it. Just say the word, the street name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blajburskih Zrtava. Bleiburg victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you had also indicated that it may have gone by a different name in 1992? Can you say that name again?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put Prekomorskih Brigada.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. I now want to talk to you about your job description. You talked about it on direct and you described for the Chamber what your role was in regard to being assistant commander for the artillery. And particularly yesterday, at page 36, you were asked: "Would it be correct to say that in relation to the command, the commander of the operation zone, you had certain advisory responsibilities?" And your answer to that question was: "That is precisely what it was, advisory responsibilities towards the commander of the operation zone." And on the same page there is another question, and it was: "And if anyone took your analysis and advice and your estimates how to take decisions and issue orders, who would that be?" And your response was: "That would be the chief of the artillery and the commander of the operation zone or the commander of the brigade or whatever units." Sir, my question for you is to just to clarify this. My question for you is: Was it your job to analyse the full military situation in the area and then give the commander advice or analysis as to the best usage of HVO artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the structure of the command was this: The commander and then Chief of Staff who integrates the work of all chiefs of branches in that command, and my role was to act as an advisor and assist in the planning, employment, training, maintenance, reinforcement and replenishment, even distribution, and regular and interim reports as required by the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In order to do that job, specifically the planning part, did you have to have knowledge of the full military situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I needed to be informed of the situation on the front line where the units of the military district organised defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked a question by Judge Antonetti at page 52, regarding whether the artillery supported the infantry and you indicated that indeed that's what the artillery did. So my question is: In order for you to effectively use artillery to support the HVO infantry in operation plans, was it important for you to know the general overall military plan for the entire municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my position of chief of artillery, I was informed of all aspects of the situation on the front line where there were units in which artillery had been deployed, artillery of the operation zone, and the focus of my information was on the disposition and the role of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you the summary given to us by Ms. Alaburic. I know you didn't write this, but I'd like you to listen. It says: "In order to understand the timing and intensity of artillery activities in the town of Mostar, it is necessary to know the overall combat activities of the ABiH and HVO in the area of the Mostar region." Now, I know you didn't write that, but would you agree with me that that's a true statement? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to talk to you specifically now about the artillery components of the HVO and you talked about this extensively yesterday, and at page 48 you were asked about the rocket artillery regiment and the question was, starting at line 14 was: "Tell us, please, at the level of the operation zone was there an artillery unit? Was there an artillery unit at the level of the operation zone?" "A. Yes. "Q. What unit was that? "A. There is a unit which was called a rocket artillery regiment, actually on its strength, it had artillery weapons that would qualify it for a reinforced battalion." "Q. What artillery tools did the regiment have at its disposal?" And your answer was: "At the beginning it had 130-millimetre cannons; 120-millimetre howitzers; D-30; and 122-D38 howitzers, two pieces; and 155-millimetre howitzer, three pieces. In total that would have been the strength of one battalion." Sir, you said this was on the operational zone level, but would you agree with me that there came a time when this unit was put directly under the Main Staff control?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's true that in a certain period this unit was placed under the operative command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you some testimony from General Praljak. It should come up on your screen on Sanction. You'll see it shortly, and this is from August 20, 2009, and regarding the same issue General Praljak spoke about it. The question then was: "Let me take you through the various units that are identified, and that's primarily what I'm interested in. The next unit that's indicated here is the rocket and artillery regiment, and it's correct, General, that pursuant to this order the rocket and artillery regiment is one of the units that's directly subordinated to the HVO Main Staff?" Praljak's answer was: "This is the artillery. This is meant to establish the full control, and that's why I asked that some of the artillery units be resubordinated and placed under the command of the Main Staff in order for us to achieve effective control to make sure they weren't doing anything outside my control." Mr. Maric, would you agree with me that it was important -- it was significant that certain important artillery items be placed directly under the Main Staff control?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If such an evaluation is made by the command, then I believe it's accurate, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were there any other artillery pieces that were directly controlled by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no other artillery pieces under control by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You're going to see more testimony in front of you and this is from August 20th. Again this is General Praljak, and this -- there was a question regarding this. The question was: "Let's just try to just sum this up. Can we agree that your intention here in this order," and we're showing a document, "in respect of the artillery, is for the Main Staff to exert greater control over the use of 130-millimetre guns, recognising that under certain circumstances it maybe appropriate for an operative zone commander to use one of these guns without first seeking permission from the Main Staff?" General Praljak's answer was: "That's right. If unable to get in touch with anybody from the Main Staff, they might just use it, under the rules." So, sir, would you agree with me at least in the case of 130-millimetre guns, that these were also pieces of artillery that came under the direct control of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during a certain time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's now turn to the brigades and the battalions, and you were asked about this yesterday as well. And at page 55, you were asked: "Can you tell us what kind of artillery weapons brigades have." And your answer was: "According to the rules, brigades usually had artillery battalions disposing of mortars up to 122-millimetres." You later corrected that to be 120. "Considering that in the operation zone we have these weapons. These weapons were placed at the disposal of artillery battalions with the proviso that some other battalions also had other calibres." So, sir, you would agree with me that, at least in regard to the brigades, they had access to 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I agree with that. In the infantry battalions there were 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then at page 56 you said specifically: "In battalions, there were mainly combat artillery groups depending on the situation in the area of responsibility that battalion. "Q. Could you give us the calibres of mortars available to such combat artillery groupings?" And your answer was: "Smaller calibre, 60 and 82 millimetres." Mr. Maric, so you would agree that even -- the battalions even had smaller mortars at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the establishment of infantry brigades, in infantry battalions or, rather, on the strength of the infantry battalions there are 60- and 82-millimetre mortars, and what I stated is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I think now we've established that in regard to the brigades and the battalions, they had mortars; 60, 82, and 120 millimetres. And then in regard to the rocket artillery regiment that was under the Main Staff, they, as you described, had 130-millimetre cannons, 120-millimetre howitzers, D30s, 122-D38s howitzers and 155 military [sic] howitzers. And then we also -- I think I've come to the conclusion that the Main Staff, at least for some time, was in role of 133-millimetre guns. Would that summary be correct, Mr. Maric? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I cannot reach my Defence counsel and things are getting complicated. You have to read my statement to the very end, and the precise answer that the Prosecutor's always repeating had a command. When and to what intent did I ask for certain artillery to be under my command and why. There are no 130-millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would that accurately sum up the state of artillery and to where it was -- under whose control it was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, the artillery in the brigades was unchanged, but the numbers of pieces varied in keeping with the circumstances on the ground, and the artillery of the rocket and artillery regiment was more often resubordinated to the command of the operation zone and there were also times when it was subordinated to the Main Staff of the HVO. I would like to join the objection given the fact that calibre not known in the artillery is mentioned. I don't want to suffer consequences as a result of that and as a result of not reacting -- reacting. If this is irrelevant, I can accept even the error because I know what the Prosecutor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, what other pieces of artillery were used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannons [as interpreted] which were part of the strength, as mentioned in the reports that I saw in Mrs. Alaburic's file. Where there was not a sufficient number of cannons as envisaged by the establishment, there could also be other pieces but with the same or similar purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, my question was --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to apologise to my learned friend Mrs. West. I would like to correct the record. On line 7 of the page in front of us, it says that the witness said cannons, but the witness said artillery pieces rather than cannons. The witness did not say cannons but artillery pieces, which means that he used a term describing something bigger or larger than just cannons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, these artillery pieces, were they under the control of the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All artillery pieces in the brigades were primarily under the control of the brigades or, rather, their commanders. In keeping with the system of subordination, the brigades were answerable to the superior command, and in our case that was the operation zone. In view of that, those pieces were under the command of the operation zone via the commanders of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will take that as a yes. Let's talk about what you just described as this system of subordination. When we consider that system of subordination or chain of command, would you agree that all of the artillery was ultimately under the chain of command directly to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units within an army are in formal terms under the Main Staff. However, their use and the command over parts of the units that form an army follow a certain scheme by the levels, and the platoon which has a mortar are also part of an army whose supreme commander is the Supreme Command. There is an organisation. The Main Staff was above all military units and districts, and military districts -- districts were composed of brigades and other units including the rocket and artillery regiment for the -- most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look to see what General Praljak said about this very issue. It's August 20th, 2009. He was asked a follow-up question: "... the other forms of weaponry, the 105 and 60s and the mortars and RPGs which remained within the brigade or the battalion, and as to those weapons, simply the question was that those were indirectly under the chain ... or remained within the chain of command of the Main Staff but they were just farther down the chain. Isn't that the correct way of putting it?" Mr. Praljak's response was: "Yes, in part. Look, everything is within the chain of command of the Main Staff. The rocket and artillery regiment, this was something for the soldier. A soldier would have been this charge of these pieces. When under attack, obviously, formally speaking, it's all within the chain of command of the Main Staff." Sir, I gather you would agree with General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with what General Praljak said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record that is transcript page 43575. Mr. Maric, did you have to issue reports to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the professional line, a chief at any level has to write reports to a higher level and receives reports from a lower level in the form and at the time prescribed by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Should I understand your answer to that question is yes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you agree that it was important to do so so that the Main Staff could exercise control?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said it, those were periodical reports which were prescribed and which had to be sent as necessary. The reports were always sent from a lower level to a higher level, and it was the higher level that prescribed their form and the time when they had to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, for example, it was important for you to ensure that the Main Staff had full knowledge of, say, the use of ammunition, because the Main Staff made decisions about its allocation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interruption, but we were going into the transcript, original transcript on the system of Mr. Praljak testimony, and it appears that the numbers of the pages which you put on the excerpt you prepared for us and which we see on the screen, those numbers does not match. They are entirely wrong. For example, on the page we are having now on the screen, on the e-court system, is 43575. Yes, 75. And here we see this is -- on this line we have the question from Mr. Stringer, and then answer, et cetera. It simply does not match. It must be some mistake. So we are not able to go into the transcript and control, or in other words, if you will later on refer to those alleged numbers, there will be complete mess because it wouldn't be clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- it cannot be, of course, corrected now, but perhaps you should correct it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. And if those are wrong, they're my fault and I will correct them. But in regard to the issue of the words themselves, those are copied directly from the transcript, but nonetheless we'll correct them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maric, my last question was, for example, it was important for you to ensure that the Main Staff had full knowledge of, say, the use of ammunition, because the Main Staff made decisions about its allocation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the Main Staff was not in charge of the replenishment of ammunition. The military district had its own logistics base, and in its depots it had certain quantities of ammunition, and my requests were sent to the logistics base of the operation zone. Actually, it was part of the briefing sessions in the military districts, which comprised officers at all levels, including logistics officers. And then based on the written or oral reports sent to the commander of the operation zone, an intervention came from the logistics base in keeping with the request that could be signed by nobody else but the commander of the operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. So we're going to look to see what General Praljak said about this issue, and this is transcript 44407. He was asked about these reports. The question was: "General, is it correct that reports were issued by the appropriate units to the Main Staff regarding the use of artillery and firing at targets in Mostar? This was an issue that was among the reports that were sent to the Main Staff." "A. Yes, for a period of time, and that mostly stayed with the operative zone, but then the number of -- amount of ammunition would be for 10 days, 15 days. You would have different reports about the amount of ammunition used, and that reached the Main Staff, too. Yes, that's right. "Q. Was it the Main Staff, then, that would have to co-ordinate the amounts of ammunition --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. "Was it the Main Staff, then, that would have to co-ordinate the amounts of ammunition, allocate amounts of ammunition, that sort of thing, to determine where the ammunition would be used and how it would be used? "A. The chief of the artillery of the Main Staff controlled the amount of ammunition used, how much ammunition there was left in the depots. So there was the chief of artillery, and in the operative zone in the Main Staff who takes care about that, and of course he reports on the situation either to me or somebody else in the Main Staff." So, Mr. Maric, you just testified that, in your view, the Main Staff was not in charge of the replenishment of ammunition. And seeing here what General Praljak said about that, do you still believe that to be the case or was General Praljak talking about something different?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have not been clear enough. I did send reports at the request of the chief of the -- to the Chief of the Main Staff about all the issues requested from the Chief of the Main Staff. From time to time, depending on the situation, those issues referred to the level of replenishment, and of course that the Chief of the Main Staff was duty-bound to report to his superiors in the Main Staff. This didn't have to be the Chief of the Main Staff, because in the Main Staff there was also the administration of each of the branches that was a single body with its own chief who communicated with the Chief of the Main Staff. I know that because in 1994, I personally was a member of that body.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall stop now because it's time. I have another trial afterwards. You have already had 35 minutes, so you have, therefore, two hours and 25 minutes left. Colonel, you shall come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
